core.text: To say that something *will be done* to someone, Latin uses **the future passive (the 'will be done' form)**. It is the future you already know (*laudābit* — he will praise) with the passive person endings on the end instead of the active ones: *laudābitur* — he will be praised. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses these same endings: *sequētur* = he will follow. Latin name: *futūrum indicātīvī passīvī*.
Passive means the subject has the action done *to* it: *the boy will be praised* (someone praises him), not *the boy will praise*.
First and second conjugation: -bor, -beris, -bitur, -bimur, -biminī, -buntur. Third and fourth: -ar, -ēris, -ētur, -ēmur, -ēminī, -entur.

invented.en: Tomorrow the letter will be written by Julius.

core.text: In the third and fourth conjugations the future passive and **the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come)** differ by one vowel: *pōnētur* (will be put) has -ē-, *pōnātur* (let it be put) has -ā-. In the first conjugation the pair is *laudābitur* (future, with *-bi-*) against *laudētur* (subjunctive, with *-ē-*).

more.text: The learner's notes (week 20) put it simply: build the future exactly as in the active, then swap in the passive endings; the -b- goes with ā- and ē-stem verbs, the a/e vowel with the rest. Watch the second person singular: *laudāberis* and *pōnēris* end in -ris, not -s.

Ørberg (cap. XX) sets the two futures side by side: the bad pupil says *laudābor, nōn reprehendar* and his father answers *nōn laudāberis, sed reprehendēris*. The rare passive infinitive of the future (*laudātum īrī*) comes later, in chapter XXIII.

teach.title: What the form does

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says what will be done to the subject?

teach.say: When what is going to happen is going to happen *to* the subject, Latin uses the future passive (the 'will be done' form): *puerī laudābuntur*, the boys will be praised. As in every passive the doer comes in behind *ā* or *ab* — *ā magistrō*, by the teacher — and the subject is the one it is done to.

check.ask: Tap the verb that says the table will have something done to it.

teach.title: The third person: -bitur and -buntur
teach.say: Take the *-b-* future of the first and second conjugations (the conjugation is which of the four families a Latin verb belongs to) and put the passive endings on it: *-bitur* for he, she or it, *-buntur* for they. *portābitur*, it will be carried; *laudābuntur*, they will be praised.

show.say: vocābitur, vocābuntur — the -b- future with a passive ending

check.ask: Now the same two cells on amō: the future passive for 'he, she, it' and for 'they'.

teach.title: The other four persons: -bor, -beris, -bimur, -biminī
teach.say: The rest of the column runs *-bor* (I), *-beris* (you), *-bimur* (we), *-biminī* (you all). The one to watch is *-beris*, with an *e* where every other person has an *i*: *verberāberis*, you will be beaten, beside *verberābitur*, he will be beaten. Everything else in the word stays as it was.

check.ask: Write the future passive of laudō for I, for you, for we and for you all.

teach.title: 3rd and 4th conjugations: -ar, then -ē-
teach.say: With no *-b-* to lean on, third- and fourth-conjugation verbs use *-ar* for 'I' (*mittar*, I will be sent) and *-ē-* for everyone else: *mittētur*, *aperiētur*. Before *-nt-* that *ē* shortens, so 'they' is *mittentur*. That long *ē* is the whole tense here: *clauditur*, it is being shut, against *claudētur*, it will be shut.

show.say: mittar for 'I'; mittētur, mittentur for the rest

check.ask: Now the same three cells on dīcō: the future passive for I, for 'he, she, it' and for 'they'.

teach.title: Deponent verbs wear these endings and mean something active
teach.say: A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses this future too, and still means something active: *sequētur* is 'he will follow', not 'he will be followed'. Read the ending for its tense and its person, and let the verb itself tell you the meaning.

check.ask: loquētur — who will be doing the talking?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Now build both patterns side by side. In the sentence in front of you the sack is the subject, the slave behind *ā* is the doer, and *portābitur* carries the future and the passive at once. Decide the conjugation first, then the person, and only then write the ending.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the future passive of pōnō, third person singular.
